chapter: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
title: From big bands to 52nd Street, Traditional Revival and tailgate style
summary: Morgenstern asks about his move to Dixieland and Sidney De Paris; Dickenson explains tailgate style and says Jazz did not only come from New Orleans.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Now, the thing that always interested me or intrigued me about your playing career is also that when you left the big band things and settled in New York and played at 52nd Street and stuff... Around that time and a little later, you had the so-called Traditional Revival thing that came in, and you started playing with Sidney Bechet and Sidney De Paris, and eventually even what you call Dixieland. And I guess you didn't play that style when you started. Did you?
I played the style that they played at that time, at the time when I started, and that was kind of like....sort of Dixieland, I would say. Yeah.
Was it what they call a tailgate style??

I don't know... "Tailgate" gets me confused. I have an idea what it is. But the word "tailgate" came from the guys sitting on the back of a wagon, and sitting out there so they could slide their horn. You know, there's no place to slide it on I guess the hay rides they used to have, and things I think. I think. I wasn't down in New

Orleans. They claim that Jazz came from New Orleans, which I don't believe. However, it was practiced more down there than it was, because there was more people...guys with horns and things down there that had a chance to learn their horns. Well, I was a country boy, and there just happened to be a horn in my house. So I just picked it up and started playing it, you know.
